title: UNSAT multi-prover proofs with efficient SAT-oracle provers
formal:
Does UNSAT have a classical multi-prover interactive proof with a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier and uniform probabilistic polynomial-time honest provers that may query SAT? The verifier has no oracle. For one fixed protocol, every unsatisfiable formula must be accepted with probability at least \(2/3\) when all provers are honest, while every satisfiable formula must be accepted with probability at most \(1/3\) for every collection of computationally unbounded, noncommunicating classical provers.

This restores the complement bar on SAT in the original Conjecture 6.2. The imported card lost that bar and incorrectly named SAT as the language to be proved; the oracle available to the honest provers is still SAT.
why: This asks whether the output of a solver for an NP-complete problem can be checked using only the computational power of that solver. It connects the trustworthiness of hard computation to interactive proofs and to the limits of reductions between NP and total search.
status_note: Source-open after a verified extraction correction: Conjecture 6.2 of the 2021 PDF uses the complement of SAT as the language and ordinary SAT as the oracle. The displayed overline was checked visually; extracted plain text and the inherited summary had lost it. The 2010 author manuscript §1.3.1 and 2025 ECCC TR25-210 §2.4 were read for the conditional program-checking connection; the latter explicitly calls SAT checkability open. Bounded later-work searches through 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution. The current review does not independently reprove the historical characterization or certify every later paper exhaustively.

progress.text: The program-checking framework and its connection to multi-prover proofs motivate the efficient-honest-prover question, explicitly restated as Conjecture 6.2 in 2021.
A randomized reduction from SAT to a total NP search oracle would imply SAT checkability; the result is conditional on the existence of that reduction.
The range-avoidance manuscript’s §2.4 still states that SAT checkability is open and recalls the TFNP implication as Theorem 2.11.

importance.reason: A longstanding program-checking question for the canonical NP-complete problem, with links to interactive proofs, total search and worst-case hardness. The honest-prover resource restriction exposes a substantial structural gap beyond ordinary coNP interactive proofs.

sentences: The actual source asks for interactive proofs of unsatisfiability, with several noncommunicating classical provers.
Honest provers must run in randomized polynomial time with SAT-oracle access, while the verifier is polynomial-time and has no oracle.
Soundness must hold against all computationally unbounded classical cheating strategies.
The target is tied to checking a purported SAT solver and remains distinct from ordinary interactive proofs with unrestricted honest provers.
The imported SAT label lost a complement bar; the card restores UNSAT and records the correction explicitly.

definitions:
Fix a binary encoding of finite Boolean formulas as explicitly written AND/OR/NOT expression trees with binary variable identifiers and delimiters. Its full bit length is \(n\). SAT consists of the well-formed formulas having a satisfying assignment. UNSAT consists of the well-formed formulas having none. The verifier rejects malformed encodings deterministically before any interaction. This convention differs from the literal language complement of SAT only on efficiently recognizable malformed strings and does not change the existence question. All participants receive the same input formula.

A protocol specifies one constant number \(k\ge2\) of provers, one uniform probabilistic polynomial-time Turing-machine verifier \(V\), and one honest probabilistic oracle Turing machine \(P_i^{\mathrm{SAT}}\) for each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\). All are fixed finite programs, independent of input length. There is one polynomial bound \(p(n)\) on the verifier’s total computation and number of fair random bits, the number of message exchanges, and the total communication bits. Each honest prover has polynomial total running time in \(n\) throughout the protocol, on every random tape and within the communication bounds; its bound may depend on the fixed protocol. Writing SAT queries and processing their answers are charged, while the oracle returns one exact satisfiability bit per invocation. Malformed oracle queries return 0. Queries are allowed to depend on the prover’s local transcript and private randomness. There is no nonuniform advice or additional oracle.

The verifier uses private random bits and sends classical messages to individually addressed provers. Each prover’s response may depend only on the common input, its identity, its own received and sent messages, and its internal random bits and state. It cannot see messages exchanged with another prover except information that the verifier explicitly forwards. Provers cannot communicate with one another once interaction starts. Classical shared randomness independent of the verifier’s private randomness is allowed: for the honest protocol, a common uniform seed of polynomial length, together with independent private fair bits, suffices to specify it. There is no entanglement or quantum communication. No constant bound on the number of rounds is required.

The verifier must respect its polynomial clock even when provers cheat. Messages longer than its prescribed bounds, invalidly formatted messages or failure to answer a requested message cause rejection. Soundness quantifies over all classical prover strategies subject only to the communication and information restrictions. Cheating provers may have unlimited computation, arbitrary input-dependent prearranged strategies and shared classical randomness; they are not limited to SAT-oracle polynomial time. For fixed input and fixed private/shared prover randomness, a strategy gives each response as a function of that prover’s local transcript. Equivalently, randomized strategies are distributions over such deterministic strategy tuples. The provers have no access to the verifier’s private bits except through the messages they receive.

Let \(\Pr[V\leftrightarrow(P_1,\ldots,P_k)(F)=1]\) mean the probability that the verifier accepts formula \(F\), over the verifier’s fair bits and the honest or cheating strategy’s randomness as applicable. The requirements are
\[\forall F\in\mathrm{UNSAT},\quad\Pr[V\leftrightarrow(P_1^{\mathrm{SAT}},\ldots,P_k^{\mathrm{SAT}})(F)=1]\ge2/3,\]
\[\forall F\in\mathrm{SAT}\ \forall(P_1^*,\ldots,P_k^*),\quad\Pr[V\leftrightarrow(P_1^*,\ldots,P_k^*)(F)=1]\le1/3.\]
One fixed tuple of honest algorithms must meet completeness for all yes-inputs. The soundness bound holds even for cheating strategies tailored separately to each no-input. Polynomial time is worst-case over randomness and allowed transcripts, not merely expected time. These constant error thresholds fix the ordinary bounded-error convention; no cryptographic hardness assumption or computational soundness restriction is allowed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof or refutation of the existence of the stated protocol. A positive answer must specify its verifier, finite prover count, honest SAT-oracle algorithms and polynomial bounds, and prove completeness and soundness against every permitted cheating strategy. A negative answer must exclude every such fixed protocol, rather than one round bound or construction. A proof system with unbounded honest provers, a verifier that can itself query SAT, efficient-cheater-only soundness, or quantum/entangled provers does not answer this target. A relativized counterexample or a consequence conditional on an unproved class separation does not refute the unrelativized statement. Exact probability inequalities and asymptotic bounds apply; numerical approximation tolerance is irrelevant.

source_formulation.text: Conjecture 6.2 asks for a multi-prover interactive proof of the complement of SAT whose honest provers use probabilistic polynomial time with a SAT oracle.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Conjecture 6.2; visually verified complement bar restored after a text-extraction error

context_blocks.text: A satisfying assignment can be checked directly, and a SAT oracle can find such an assignment by deciding successive partial assignments. Consequently, the analogous efficient-prover statement for satisfiable formulas is straightforward. Certifying unsatisfiability is the substantive target; losing the complement bar changes the mathematical question.

Several provers can be cross-examined while being prevented from coordinating their answers during the interaction. The verifier remains computationally weak. The extra requirement here is that honest provers can prepare all their responses using only randomized polynomial time with SAT decisions, while dishonest provers receive no computational restriction.

The source relates this protocol to SAT program checking. In that setting a randomized polynomial-time checker can query a purported solver: it must flag an error with high probability if the answer on the designated input is wrong, and accept the answer with high probability if the solver is correct on all inputs. Correctness only on the designated input need not force acceptance.

Fortnow states the characterization connecting checkability to efficient-oracle-prover multi-prover proofs for a language and its complement. The SAT side is straightforward; the UNSAT side is the unresolved requirement. Ordinary interactive proofs for coNP with unrestricted honest prover computation do not establish this stronger efficiency statement.

Mahmoody and Xiao record the implication \(\mathrm{SAT}\in\mathrm{BPP}^{\mathrm{TFNP}}\Rightarrow\mathrm{SAT}\text{ is checkable}\). Here TFNP consists of total search relations with polynomially bounded, polynomial-time-checkable solutions, and the antecedent means that a randomized polynomial-time SAT algorithm can use an oracle returning any valid solution of one such relation. The antecedent is not known, so this is a conditional connection rather than a protocol satisfying the card.

The 2025 range-avoidance paper explicitly retains SAT checkability as open in its §2.4 and recalls the same conditional implication. Its new protocols concern range avoidance and circuit image sizes; that discussion does not assert the requested UNSAT protocol.
